editorial.text: A library visitor once complimented me by saying that my library did not have the “stench of death”. He meant that the library’s appearance showed that the place was still valued. There was no damage outside or graffiti and interior was warm and welcoming with up to date displays and very little fossilised blue-tack on the walls. The thing is, though, I know libraries with that smell. I have been to libraries where the council, not mine thank goodness, clearly does not care and, sadly, the library teams have been unable to keep up their morale. This lethal infection starts from the head: if the council does not invest in its libraries then sooner or later – and it can take decades – the local library starts looking awful. And people don’t come in, and the vicious circle of decline in investment and in usage becomes evident. But this does not need to be the case. A well-maintained and attractive building, with money enough to change with the times, will lead to a thriving library. But where does the money come from? Well, ultimately, from central government, either through direct grant or through sufficiently funding councils. And this has not happened sufficiently in decades, Since the start of this website in 2010, we have had a decade of austerity – where the already-insufficient funding in infrastructure has been cut – followed by years where funding has been stable but has not taken into account inflation or the demands of social welfare. Many of us were excited when a new party came to power, but it quickly became apparent under Starmer that nothing would change. And now there is renewed hope for the new prime minister, but the budget this week showed a slight change in the mood music at least. A good a time in a decade or two to ask for money then. But in order to do this, we need to know how much we want, so the new Arup and Designing Libraries Collaboration is to be welcomed. This will “establish the first comprehensive assessment of library capital investment requirements in almost two decades.” It’s been done before – the 2006 report identified £760 million was needed – but then in 2010 it all became moot when the Government made clear none of it was going to happen. But that was 20 years ago. A recent similar project Evaluating Capital Investment Needs for Arts Centres in the UK was quoted in this year’s Hodge Review and may have influenced Lisa Nandy. So how will it work? Inevitably, it’s all voluntary. Individual councils will be asked for what is needed and it is to be hoped that they will answer honestly and that they will see it’s in their best interest to do so. And if some councils don’t get involved because the figure is too embarrassing for them … well, at least we will know where the smell is coming from. Please email me at ianlibrarian@live.co.uk with any news and views or if you wish to advertise. Subscription is free by using the box on the right-hand side.

Value of libraries cannot be measured by ‘loans and visitor numbers’ – RUV. “The chair of Félag librarfræðinga (the Association of Librarians) says the benefits libraries bring to society go far beyond what can be measured in borrowing figures and visitor numbers. She cannot see how library services can be streamlined and improved at the same time. The majority on Reykjavík City Council’s Culture Committee has proposed a comprehensive review of the operations, activities and future organisation of Reykjavík City Library (Reykjavík City Library). The proposal calls for a quantitative comparison of operating costs and the use of premises. Costs per visitor and per book loan would be examined, along with the possibility of reducing the number of library branches.”

stories.text: A new book revisits the years when Bombay’s working-class libraries were flourishing – Scroll. “As Bombay expanded in the late 19th century and early 20th century, it developed a strong library culture, which came to be organised along various lines – religious communities, neighbourhoods, and secular educational institutions. On the one hand, there were community-led libraries, such as the Mulla Firoz Library (established in 1830), containing books relating to Zoroastrian religion, the Jain Reading Room and Library, the Jamestji Nasarwanji Petit Fore Reading Room and Library by Parsis, the MJ Khoja Library and the Anjuman-i-Islam by Muslims. On the other hand, there were strong neighbourhood libraries, such as the Native General Library (established in 1845) in Dhobi Talao and Sr D Petit Khanda Mohalla Library in Nizampura.”

stories.text: Book? – Santa Barbara Independent. “An individual consumer pays about $13 on average for an e-book and receives ongoing access. A public library typically pays $55 or more for a license that may last only two years and allow only one reader at a time to borrow the book. When the license expires, the library may have to pay again to continue providing the same title. This challenge is being felt here at home. At the Santa Barbara Public Library, digital materials are provided through several different licensing models, many of which expire after two years.”

stories.text: London Now. “Imagine this reader, at the click of a button, every public library in the UK is lost, destroyed, forgotten. Would you even notice this change? Well according to the Arts Council England, only 30% of the general public (aged over 16) have used public libraries in the last year. To put this in perspective, in 2006, roughly half of the adult population in the UK had used public libraries that year. This drastic decline has been often attributed to the increasing use of modern technology such as Mobile phones and ebooks, leading to less people actually needing to use a physical book. Does this mean that modern public libraries are obsolete?” … “change is inevitable and thus libraries no longer have the purpose of holding information, but rather now have a duty of providing a safe space for people to hang out, to have fun and to read.”

To put this in perspective, in 2006, roughly half of the adult population in the UK had used public libraries that year. This drastic decline has been often attributed to the increasing use of modern technology such as Mobile phones and ebooks, leading to less people actually needing to use a physical book. Does this mean that modern public libraries are obsolete?” … “change is inevitable and thus libraries no longer have the purpose of holding information, but rather now have a duty of providing a safe space for people to hang out, to have fun and to read.”
